summary: Garenoxacin is a des-fluoro(6) quinolone (often grouped with the fluoroquinolones) with broad activity against Gram-positive organisms (including Streptococcus pneumoniae), Gram-negative bacteria, atypical respiratory pathogens, and anaerobes. It is used for community respiratory tract infections and other susceptible bacterial infections in countries where it is approved (notably Japan). The usual oral dose is around 400 mg once daily. As a quinolone, it shares class warnings including tendinitis/tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, QT-interval prolongation, blood-glucose disturbances, and aggravation of myasthenia gravis. Garenoxacin is NOT FDA-approved (its U.S. development was discontinued); dosing and labelling follow the approved regional product information.
indications: Community-acquired respiratory tract infections (e.g., pneumonia, acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis, sinusitis) caused by susceptible organisms
Other susceptible bacterial infections (e.g., otolaryngological and certain skin/soft-tissue infections) per the approved regional label

dosage.n: Duration per indication and regional product information

dosage.d: Reduce dose/extend interval in significant renal impairment per local label
dosage.n: Verify against the approved product information

dosage.d: Usual dose with attention to renal function and QT/tendon risk
dosage.n: Higher class risk of tendon and cardiac effects

admin: Take orally once daily, with or without food
Separate from antacids, sucralfate, multivitamins, and products containing magnesium, aluminium, calcium, iron, or zinc by several hours (cations reduce absorption)
Complete the full prescribed course even if symptoms improve
Avoid in patients with risk factors for QT prolongation or significant tendon disorders where possible
moa: Garenoxacin is a quinolone antibacterial that inhibits the bacterial type II topoisomerases DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, enzymes essential for bacterial DNA replication, transcription, repair, and recombination. By binding these enzyme-DNA complexes it blocks DNA supercoiling and strand separation, leading to lethal disruption of bacterial DNA synthesis and a bactericidal effect. It lacks the C-6 fluorine of classical fluoroquinolones (a des-fluoro quinolone) yet retains broad-spectrum activity, including against many Gram-positive, Gram-negative, atypical, and anaerobic organisms.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to garenoxacin or other quinolones
Children/adolescents (quinolone class - articular cartilage concern), except where specifically justified
relative: History of tendon disorders related to quinolone use
Risk factors for QT prolongation (electrolyte disturbance, concomitant QT-prolonging drugs, significant cardiac disease)
Epilepsy or CNS disorders lowering seizure threshold
monitor: QT interval/cardiac status in at-risk patients

preg: As with quinolones generally, garenoxacin is not recommended in pregnancy because of class concerns about effects on developing cartilage and limited human safety data. Use a suitable alternative antibacterial in pregnant patients.
lact: Quinolones are generally avoided during breastfeeding due to potential effects on the infant. Garenoxacin is not recommended during lactation; if treatment is essential, consider an alternative agent or interruption of breastfeeding.
renal: Garenoxacin is partly eliminated renally, so dose reduction or interval extension may be required in significant renal impairment. Follow the approved regional product information and monitor renal function in at-risk patients.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; data are limited. Monitor for signs of hepatotoxicity and follow local prescribing guidance.

major: QT-prolonging drugs (class IA/III antiarrhythmics, certain antipsychotics, macrolides) - additive risk of QT prolongation/arrhythmia
Multivalent cations (antacids, sucralfate, iron, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc) - markedly reduce absorption; separate dosing
moderate: NSAIDs - may increase CNS stimulation/seizure risk with quinolones
Antidiabetic agents/insulin - quinolones can cause hypo- or hyperglycaemia; monitor glucose
Corticosteroids - increased tendon rupture risk, especially in the elderly
minor: Caffeine and theophylline - quinolones may variably affect metabolism; monitor for toxicity
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food, but separate from cation-containing products (dairy, antacids, mineral supplements) by several hours.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction; limit alcohol, particularly in acutely unwell patients.
interactions.diagnostics: May affect blood glucose readings; consider baseline ECG in patients at risk of QT prolongation.

rare: Severe cutaneous reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis)

monitoring: Clinical response and signs of superinfection (including C. difficile)
Tendon symptoms - stop the drug and rest the limb if pain/inflammation occurs
Cardiac/QT risk and blood glucose in susceptible patients
counsel: Take once daily and finish the whole course, even when you feel better
Do not take it within a few hours of antacids, iron, calcium, zinc, or dairy products - they stop it working
Stop the medicine and contact your doctor if you get tendon pain or swelling (especially the back of the ankle), numbness/tingling, or unusual mood/confusion
Avoid prolonged sun exposure and report any rash or blistering
Tell your doctor about heart rhythm problems, low potassium/magnesium, myasthenia gravis, or diabetes, and report fainting/palpitations or unexpected low/high blood sugars
pk: Antibacterial effect begins shortly after absorption; clinical improvement over days
Plasma concentration peaks within a few hours of an oral dose
Long terminal half-life (reported around 12-18 hours) supporting once-daily dosing
Store at controlled room temperature, protected from moisture; keep in original packaging
pearls: Not FDA-approved - U.S. development of garenoxacin was discontinued; it is approved in Japan (and some other markets). Dosing/labelling follow the approved regional product information rather than an FDA label
A des-fluoro(6) quinolone - lacks the classical C-6 fluorine but is grouped with fluoroquinolones and shares their class warnings
Class quinolone cautions apply: tendinitis/rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, QT prolongation, dysglycaemia, and myasthenia gravis aggravation
Broad spectrum including S. pneumoniae, atypical pathogens, and anaerobes - useful in respiratory infection where approved
Separate dosing from antacids and multivalent cations, which markedly reduce absorption
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with the usual once-daily schedule. Do not take a double dose. Complete the full course as prescribed.
overdose: There is no specific antidote. Manage overdose with supportive and symptomatic care, ensure adequate hydration, and monitor cardiac rhythm (QT interval), CNS status, and glucose. Remove unabsorbed drug from the gastrointestinal tract where appropriate. Haemodialysis is unlikely to remove significant amounts. Treat seizures and arrhythmias with standard measures.
